claim: Ddb1 is highly expressed in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Ddb1 is highly expressed in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors and its deletion leads to abrogation of both adult and fetal hematopoiesis, targeting specifically transiently amplifying progenitor subsets.
evidence: Supported by expression analysis data presented in the manuscript showing Ddb1 expression levels in different hematopoietic populations.

claim: Ddb1 deletion leads to abrogation of both adult and fetal hematopoiesis.
source: Ddb1 is highly expressed in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors and its deletion leads to abrogation of both adult and fetal hematopoiesis, targeting specifically transiently amplifying progenitor subsets.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Ddb1 deletion in mouse models showing loss of hematopoietic function.

claim: Ddb1 deletion specifically targets transiently amplifying progenitor subsets.
source: Ddb1 is highly expressed in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors and its deletion leads to abrogation of both adult and fetal hematopoiesis, targeting specifically transiently amplifying progenitor subsets.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing differential effects on progenitor populations versus quiescent stem cells.

claim: Ddb1 deletion in non-dividing lymphocytes has no discernible phenotypes.
source: However, Ddb1 deletion in non-dividing lymphocytes has no discernible phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CD4Cre-mediated deletion showing normal T cell development and homeostasis.

claim: Ddb1 silencing activates Trp53 pathway.
source: Ddb1 silencing activates Trp53 pathway and leads to significant effects on cell cycle progression and rapid apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased phospho-Trp53 levels and upregulation of Trp53 target genes.

claim: Ddb1 silencing leads to significant effects on cell cycle progression.
source: Ddb1 silencing activates Trp53 pathway and leads to significant effects on cell cycle progression and rapid apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation and CFSE dilution assays showing impaired cell cycle entry.

claim: Ddb1 silencing leads to rapid apoptosis.
source: Ddb1 silencing activates Trp53 pathway and leads to significant effects on cell cycle progression and rapid apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV staining and TUNEL assays showing increased apoptosis in Ddb1-deficient cells.

claim: The abrogation of hematopoietic progenitor cells can be partially rescued by simultaneous deletion of Trp53.
source: The abrogation of hematopoietic progenitor cells can be partially rescued by simultaneous deletion of Trp53.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Trp53-/-::Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice showing partial restoration of progenitor cell numbers.

claim: Depletion of DDB1 in embryonic stem cell (ESC) leads to differentiation.
source: Conversely, depletion of DDB1 in embryonic stem cell (ESC) leads to differentiation albeit negative effects on cell cycle and apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing downregulation of pluripotency markers and upregulation of differentiation markers.

claim: DDB1 depletion in ESC does not have negative effects on cell cycle and apoptosis.
source: Conversely, depletion of DDB1 in embryonic stem cell (ESC) leads to differentiation albeit negative effects on cell cycle and apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing no significant changes in cell cycle distribution or apoptosis rates in ESC.

claim: Mass spectrometry reveals differing protein interactions between DDB1 and distinct DCAFs between cell types.
source: Mass spectrometry reveals differing protein interactions between DDB1 and distinct DCAFs, the substrate recognizing components of the E3 complex, between cell types.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data identifying different DCAF proteins in ESC, 293T, and HL60 cells.

claim: CUL4-DDB1 complex is a novel post-translational regulator of stem and progenitor maintenance and differentiation.
source: Our studies identify CUL4-DDB1 complex as a novel post-translational regulator of stem and progenitor maintenance and differentiation.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive experimental data showing effects of DDB1 deletion on multiple stem cell types.

claim: Stem cells possess the unique properties of self-renewal and the capacity to differentiate to multiple cell types.
source: Stem cells posses the unique properties of self-renewal and the capacity to differentiate to multiple cell types.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about stem cell biology.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) are rare and specialized cells which are able to give rise to all blood lineages.
source: In the case of hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) they are rare and specialized cells, which are able to give rise to all blood lineages.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSC biology.

claim: The balance between HSC self-renewal and differentiation needs to be tightly regulated to keep the HSC pool size and constantly replenish mature blood cells.
source: The balance between HSC self-renewal and differentiation needs to be tightly regulated in order to keep the HSC pool size as well as to constantly replenish mature blood cells (Orkin and Zon, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on HSC regulation.

claim: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines.
source: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines (Zsebo et al., 1990; de Sauvage et al., 1996) and developmental signals (Stier et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003) and intrinsically by transcription factors (Wilson et al., 2004; Tothova et al., 2007; Reavie et al., 2010), cell cycle regulators (Cheng et al., 2000) and metabolic pathways (Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on HSC regulation.

claim: HSC function is governed extrinsically by developmental signals.
source: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines (Zsebo et al., 1990; de Sauvage et al., 1996) and developmental signals (Stier et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003) and intrinsically by transcription factors (Wilson et al., 2004; Tothova et al., 2007; Reavie et al., 2010), cell cycle regulators (Cheng et al., 2000) and metabolic pathways (Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on HSC regulation.

claim: HSC function is governed intrinsically by transcription factors.
source: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines (Zsebo et al., 1990; de Sauvage et al., 1996) and developmental signals (Stier et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003) and intrinsically by transcription factors (Wilson et al., 2004; Tothova et al., 2007; Reavie et al., 2010), cell cycle regulators (Cheng et al., 2000) and metabolic pathways (Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on HSC regulation.

claim: HSC function is governed intrinsically by cell cycle regulators.
source: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines (Zsebo et al., 1990; de Sauvage et al., 1996) and developmental signals (Stier et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003) and intrinsically by transcription factors (Wilson et al., 2004; Tothova et al., 2007; Reavie et al., 2010), cell cycle regulators (Cheng et al., 2000) and metabolic pathways (Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on HSC regulation.

claim: HSC function is governed intrinsically by metabolic pathways.
source: HSC function is governed extrinsically by cytokines (Zsebo et al., 1990; de Sauvage et al., 1996) and developmental signals (Stier et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003) and intrinsically by transcription factors (Wilson et al., 2004; Tothova et al., 2007; Reavie et al., 2010), cell cycle regulators (Cheng et al., 2000) and metabolic pathways (Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on HSC regulation.

claim: Little is known about how HSCs are regulated at the post-translational level.
source: However, little is known about how HSCs are regulated at the post-translational level.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field at the time of publication.

claim: The ubiquitin-dependent proteasome degradation system (UPS) is a primary mechanism that controls protein turnover and activation.
source: The ubiquitin-dependent proteasome degradation system (UPS) is a primary mechanism that controls protein turnover and activation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the UPS system.

claim: UPS acts via three sequential enzymes: an E1 ubiquitin activating enzyme, an E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme and an E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: UPS acts via three sequential enzymes: an E1 ubiquitin activating enzyme, an E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme and an E3 ubiquitin ligase (Crusio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligases confer substrate specificity.
source: Among these three enzymes, E3 ubiquitin ligases confer substrate specificity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about E3 ligase function.

claim: Fbw7 governs quiescence of HSCs.
source: In HSCs, it has been shown that Fbw7, an E3 ubiquitin ligase member, governs quiescence of HSCs (Matsuoka et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Itch and c-Cbl negatively regulate HSC homeostasis and function.
source: Itch and c-Cbl, other two E3 ubiquitin ligases, have been reported to negatively regulate HSC homeostasis and function (Rathinam et al., 2008; Rathinam et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Huwe1 regulates proliferation and differentiation of neural progenitor cells as well as embryonic stem cells.
source: In other stem cell systems, it has been shown that Huwe1, a HECT domain containing E3 ubiquitin ligase, regulates proliferation and differentiation of neural progenitor cells as well as embryonic stem cells (ESC) (D'Arca et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Protein levels of OCT4 and NANOG are modulated in an ubiquitin-dependent manner.
source: Protein levels of OCT4 and NANOG, transcription factors required for pluripotency, are modulated in an ubiquitin-dependent manner (Xu et al., 2009; Ramakrishna et al., 2011; Buckley et al., 2012), suggesting key roles of E3 ligase complexes for ESC differentiation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: DNA damage binding protein 1 (Ddb1) is a component of the Cullin4-containing E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: DNA damage binding protein 1 (Ddb1), a component of the Cullin4-containing E3 ubiquitin ligase, was originally identified as a protein involved in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DDB1.

claim: DDB1 was originally identified as a protein involved in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.
source: DNA damage binding protein 1 (Ddb1), a component of the Cullin4-containing E3 ubiquitin ligase, was originally identified as a protein involved in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DDB1.

claim: DDB1 heterodimerizes with DDB2 and shows high affinity for UV-induced DNA damage sites.
source: DDB1 heterodimerizes with DDB2 and shows high affinity for UV-induced DNA damage sites (Batty et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 complex ubiquitinates DDB2 and targets it for degradation, facilitating subsequent repair events.
source: Once bound to a damaged site, the CUL4-DDB1 complex ubiquitinates DDB2 and targets it for degradation, facilitating subsequent repair events (Sugasawa et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: CUL4A or CUL4B binds to the RING finger protein to interact with the E2 conjugating enzyme through its C-terminus.
source: Through its C-terminus, CUL4A or CUL4B binds to the RING finger protein to interact with the E2 conjugating enzyme.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CUL4 structure and function.

claim: CUL4A or CUL4B binds to DDB1 on its N-terminus to recruit CUL4-DDB1 associated factors (DCAF).
source: On its N-terminus, CUL4A or CUL4B binds to DDB1 to recruit CUL4-DDB1 associated factors (DCAF), a family of WD40 repeat proteins which confer substrate specificity (Angers et al., 2006; He et al., 2006; Higa et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: DCAF proteins are a family of WD40 repeat proteins which confer substrate specificity.
source: On its N-terminus, CUL4A or CUL4B binds to DDB1 to recruit CUL4-DDB1 associated factors (DCAF), a family of WD40 repeat proteins which confer substrate specificity (Angers et al., 2006; He et al., 2006; Higa et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 ligase targets the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 for ubiquitin dependent degradation.
source: The list of substrates include the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Higa et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2004), the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 (Bondar et al., 2006) and Cdkn1aCip1 (Abbas et al., 2008; Nishitani et al., 2008), the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 (Oda et al., 2010; Tardat et al., 2010), and Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast (Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 ligase targets the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 for ubiquitin dependent degradation.
source: The list of substrates include the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Higa et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2004), the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 (Bondar et al., 2006) and Cdkn1aCip1 (Abbas et al., 2008; Nishitani et al., 2008), the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 (Oda et al., 2010; Tardat et al., 2010), and Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast (Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 ligase targets Cdkn1aCip1 for ubiquitin dependent degradation.
source: The list of substrates include the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Higa et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2004), the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 (Bondar et al., 2006) and Cdkn1aCip1 (Abbas et al., 2008; Nishitani et al., 2008), the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 (Oda et al., 2010; Tardat et al., 2010), and Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast (Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 ligase targets the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 for ubiquitin dependent degradation.
source: The list of substrates include the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Higa et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2004), the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 (Bondar et al., 2006) and Cdkn1aCip1 (Abbas et al., 2008; Nishitani et al., 2008), the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 (Oda et al., 2010; Tardat et al., 2010), and Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast (Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 ligase targets Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast, for ubiquitin dependent degradation.
source: The list of substrates include the DNA replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Higa et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2004), the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 (Bondar et al., 2006) and Cdkn1aCip1 (Abbas et al., 2008; Nishitani et al., 2008), the histone methyltransferase PR-Set7 (Oda et al., 2010; Tardat et al., 2010), and Epe1, a JmjC domain-containing histone demethylase in fission yeast (Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The CUL4-DDB1 complex can be modulated by binding of the drug lenalidomide leading to degradation of lymphoid transcription factors IKZF1 and IKF3 in multiple myeloma cells.
source: More recently it has been found that the CUL4-DDB1 complex can be modulated by binding of the drug, lenalidomide leading to degradation of lymphoid transcription factors IKZF1 and IKF3 in multiple myeloma cells (Fischer et al., 2014; Kronke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Germline Cul4a deleted mice are viable and display no gross abnormality.
source: Intriguingly, germline Cul4a deleted mice are viable and display no gross abnormality (Liu et al., 2009), possibly due to redundancy with Cul4b, whereas Ddb1 deletion is embryonic lethal and embryos are not seen past E12.5 (Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ddb1 deletion is embryonic lethal and embryos are not seen past E12.5.
source: Intriguingly, germline Cul4a deleted mice are viable and display no gross abnormality (Liu et al., 2009), possibly due to redundancy with Cul4b, whereas Ddb1 deletion is embryonic lethal and embryos are not seen past E12.5 (Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Cul4a in the skin leads to resistance to UV-induced skin carcinogenesis.
source: Conditional inactivation of Cul4a in the skin leads to resistance to UV-induced skin carcinogenesis (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Specific deletion of Ddb1 in brain results in elimination of neuronal progenitor cells, hemorrhages in brain, and neonatal lethality.
source: Specific deletion of Ddb1 in brain results in elimination of neuronal progenitor cells, hemorrhages in brain, and neonatal lethality (Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: DDB1 plays a role in ESC self-renewal.
source: DDB1 also plays a role in ESC self-renewal, and silencing of Ddb1 led ESC to differentiate (Buckley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Silencing of Ddb1 led ESC to differentiate.
source: DDB1 also plays a role in ESC self-renewal, and silencing of Ddb1 led ESC to differentiate (Buckley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ddb1 loss impairs HSPC function in both the adult bone marrow and the fetal liver.
source: Here we report that Ddb1 loss impairs HSPC function in both the adult bone marrow and the fetal liver.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional deletion experiments in both adult and fetal hematopoiesis.

claim: Ddb1 deletion leads to induction of DNA damage.
source: More specifically, Ddb1 deletion leads to induction of DNA damage, rapid induction of apoptosis, and Trp53 response, resulting in bone marrow failure and acute lethality.
evidence: Supported by γH2Ax staining and 53BP1 foci data.

claim: Ddb1 deletion leads to rapid induction of apoptosis.
source: More specifically, Ddb1 deletion leads to induction of DNA damage, rapid induction of apoptosis, and Trp53 response, resulting in bone marrow failure and acute lethality.
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV staining and TUNEL assay data.

claim: Ddb1 deletion leads to Trp53 response.
source: More specifically, Ddb1 deletion leads to induction of DNA damage, rapid induction of apoptosis, and Trp53 response, resulting in bone marrow failure and acute lethality.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased phospho-Trp53 and Cdkn1a expression.

claim: Ddb1 deletion results in bone marrow failure and acute lethality.
source: More specifically, Ddb1 deletion leads to induction of DNA damage, rapid induction of apoptosis, and Trp53 response, resulting in bone marrow failure and acute lethality.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data and bone marrow cellularity analysis.

claim: Deletion of Ddb1 had no effect on resting mature lymphoid cells.
source: However, deletion of Ddb1 had no effect on resting mature lymphoid cells and whereas in proliferating embryonic stem cells (ESC) silencing of Ddb1 led to loss of pluripotency without effects on cell survival.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from CD4Cre-mediated deletion showing normal T cell development.

claim: In proliferating embryonic stem cells (ESC) silencing of Ddb1 led to loss of pluripotency without effects on cell survival.
source: However, deletion of Ddb1 had no effect on resting mature lymphoid cells and whereas in proliferating embryonic stem cells (ESC) silencing of Ddb1 led to loss of pluripotency without effects on cell survival.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing loss of pluripotency markers and flow cytometry data showing no change in apoptosis.

claim: Several E3 ligases are among the top 20% highly expressed genes in LSK cells.
source: To study the role of distinct ubiquitin ligases in the biology of HSCs, we initially performed a meta-analysis of genome-wide expression in lineage-Sca1+cKit+ (LSK) cells, a population enriched for HSCs, and found several E3 ligases among the top 20% highly expressed genes, including the already reported HSC regulators Fbw7 (Thompson et al., 2008), Cul1, Itch (Rathinam et al., 2011) and c-Cbl (Rathinam et al., 2008) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by microarray expression data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Both genes of the Cul4DDB1 complex were highly expressed in LSKs.
source: Both genes of the Cul4DDB1 complex were also highly expressed in LSKs (Figure 1a), suggesting that this E3 complex could be important in early hematopoiesis.
evidence: Supported by microarray expression data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Ddb1 was expressed at a low level in quiescent LT-HSCs.
source: It was found that Ddb1 was expressed at a low level in quiescent LT-HSCs, and significantly upregulated in multipotent progenitors (MPP, CD150-CD48+LSK), a proliferating progenitor subset.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ddb1 was significantly upregulated in multipotent progenitors (MPP), a proliferating progenitor subset.
source: It was found that Ddb1 was expressed at a low level in quiescent LT-HSCs, and significantly upregulated in multipotent progenitors (MPP, CD150-CD48+LSK), a proliferating progenitor subset.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ddb1 expression remained constant in later progenitor populations.
source: Ddb1 expression remained constant in later progenitor populations (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The Vav1 promoter drives the expression of Cre recombinase in entire hematopoietic compartment during embryonic development (~E13.5) from HSC and progenitors to mature cells.
source: The Vav1 promoter drives the expression of Cre recombinase in entire hematopoietic compartment during embryonic development (~E13.5) from HSC and progenitors to mature cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Vav1Cre mouse model.

claim: Efficient deletion of Ddb1 in bone marrow was confirmed by qPCR.
source: Efficient deletion of Ddb1 in bone marrow was confirmed by qPCR (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice were born at normal frequencies and were indistinguishable from littermates.
source: Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice were born at normal frequencies and were indistinguishable from littermates.
evidence: Supported by observation of birth frequencies.

claim: Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ animals died rapidly after birth.
source: However, Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ animals died rapidly after birth (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice had significantly decreased counts of white blood cells, red blood cells and platelets compared to littermates at day 7.
source: Peripheral blood analysis at day 7 showed that Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice had significantly decreased counts of white blood cells, red blood cells and platelets compared to littermates (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood count data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: The cellularity and size of thymus and spleen were significantly reduced in Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice.
source: Moreover, the cellularity and size of thymus and spleen were significantly reduced (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: Supported by cell count and organ size data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: Lineage-Sca1+cKit+ (LSK) cells and cKit+ progenitors were undetectable in Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice.
source: When analyzed by flow cytometry, lineage-Sca1+cKit+ (LSK) cells, a population enriched for HSCs, and cKit+ progenitors were undetectable (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Mature lymphoid and myeloid cells were severely reduced in Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice.
source: Mature lymphoid (CD4+CD8+ in thymus, B220+IgM+ in spleen) and myeloid (Gr1+Mac1+ in spleen) cells were severely reduced (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Vav1Cre expression starts as early as embryonic day 13.5 (E13.5).
source: Since Vav1Cre expression starts as early as embryonic day 13.5 (E13.5) (Stadtfeld and Graf, 2005), we hypothesized that the pan-cytopenia in Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ neonates was due to defects initiated during fetal hematopoiesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Deletion of Ddb1 in fetal hematopoietic cells led to reduction of the LSK and cKit+ progenitors, as well as mature CD19+ B-lymphoid and Gr1+ myeloid cells.
source: Analysis of E16.5 fetal liver of Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ mice showed that the deletion of Ddb1 in fetal hematopoietic cells led to reduction of the LSK and cKit+ progenitors, as well as mature CD19+ B-lymphoid and Gr1+ myeloid cells (Figure 2i).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from E16.5 fetal liver shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The distribution of LT-HSC and MPP was skewed with higher frequency of LT-HSC and lower frequency of MPP cells in Ddb1f/f::Vav1Cre+ fetal liver.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of LT-HSC and MPP was skewed with higher frequency of LT-HSC and lower frequency of MPP cells (Figure 2i).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Ddb1-deficient LSKs up-regulated genes associated with stem cell identity (Mecom, Thy1, Angpt1).
source: Genome-wide gene expression analysis revealed that Ddb1-deficient LSKs up-regulated genes associated with stem cell identity (Mecom, Thy1, Angpt1) and down-regulated genes associated with differentiation (Figure 2j,k), consistent with the phenotypic enrichment of the HSC population.
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2j,k.

claim: Ddb1-deficient LSKs down-regulated genes associated with differentiation.
source: Genome-wide gene expression analysis revealed that Ddb1-deficient LSKs up-regulated genes associated with stem cell identity (Mecom, Thy1, Angpt1) and down-regulated genes associated with differentiation (Figure 2j,k), consistent with the phenotypic enrichment of the HSC population.
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2j,k.

claim: The floxed allele of Ddb1 was recombined efficiently after polyI:C injection in all hematopoietic tissues including the bone marrow.
source: The floxed allele of Ddb1 was recombined efficiently after polyI:C injection in all hematopoietic tissues including the bone marrow (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The Ddb1 protein was undetectable in polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ bone marrow.
source: As a result, the Ddb1 protein was undetectable in polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ bone marrow (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: All Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ animals died within 3 weeks post Ddb1 deletion.
source: Strikingly, all Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ animals died within 3 weeks post Ddb1 deletion (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Ddb1 loss resulted in significant reduction in the total number of white blood cells and platelets 7 days after polyI:C injection.
source: Peripheral blood counts showed that the Ddb1 loss resulted in significant reduction in the total number of white blood cells and platelets (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood count data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: No reduction was found in red blood cells 7 days after Ddb1 deletion.
source: No reduction was found in red blood cells, however enucleated red blood cells have a half-life of approximately 40 days suggesting DDB1 deficient mice succumb to hematopoietic failure prior to red blood cell turnover.
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood count data and inference about RBC half-life.

claim: Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ bone marrow hypo-cellularity was evident from histological examination.
source: Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ bone marrow hypo-cellularity was evident from histological examination (Figure 3e), which was mostly accounted by cellularity decrease of myeloid lineage (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Bone marrow hypo-cellularity was mostly accounted by cellularity decrease of myeloid lineage.
source: Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ bone marrow hypo-cellularity was evident from histological examination (Figure 3e), which was mostly accounted by cellularity decrease of myeloid lineage (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: cKit+ progenitors (both MP and LSK) were decreased in cell number at day 5 and further more at day 7 after Ddb1 deletion.
source: cKit+ progenitors (both MP and LSK) were decreased in cell number at day 5 and further more at day 7 (Figure 3h,i).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3h,i.

claim: The frequencies of LT-HSC, ST-HSC and MPP subsets were distorted upon Ddb1 deletion, with significant relative over-representation of LT-HSCs.
source: It was found that the frequencies of LT-HSC, ST-HSC and MPP subsets were distorted upon Ddb1 deletion, as there was a significant relative over-representation of LT-HSCs (Figure 3h), similar to the findings in fetal hematopoiesis.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: MPPs, but not ST- and LT-HSCs, were decreased at day5 after Ddb1 deletion.
source: In terms of cell number, MPPs, but not ST- and LT-HSCs, were decreased at day5, which was followed by the decrease of all HSPCs subsets at day7 (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: All HSPC subsets were decreased at day7 after Ddb1 deletion.
source: In terms of cell number, MPPs, but not ST- and LT-HSCs, were decreased at day5, which was followed by the decrease of all HSPCs subsets at day7 (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: The Cre recombinase under control of the Mx1 promoter is expressed in other IFNα-responsive tissues besides hematopoietic cells, including the liver, lungs, and heart.
source: The Cre recombinase under control of the Mx1 promoter is also expressed in other IFNα-responsive tissues besides hematopoietic cells, including the liver, lungs, and heart (Kuhn et al., 1995), however no gross abnormality was found in Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice at the time-point of the analysis (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: No gross abnormality was found in non-hematopoietic tissues of Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice at the time-point of the analysis.
source: The Cre recombinase under control of the Mx1 promoter is also expressed in other IFNα-responsive tissues besides hematopoietic cells, including the liver, lungs, and heart (Kuhn et al., 1995), however no gross abnormality was found in Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice at the time-point of the analysis (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by observation of tissues.

claim: The majority of chimeric Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice with wild type bone marrow survived significantly longer than Ddb1 deficient mice.
source: In this case, the majority of chimeric Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice survived significantly longer than Ddb1 deficient mice (Figure 3j), strongly suggesting that the acute lethality observed in polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice is due to bone marrow ablation.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The acute lethality observed in polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice is due to bone marrow ablation.
source: In this case, the majority of chimeric Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice survived significantly longer than Ddb1 deficient mice (Figure 3j), strongly suggesting that the acute lethality observed in polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ mice is due to bone marrow ablation.
evidence: Supported by survival data from bone marrow transplant experiments shown in Figure 3j.

claim: DDB1 deficient bone marrow cells were not able to form colonies in cytokine-supplemented in vitro culture.
source: Strikingly, DDB1 deficient bone marrow cells from polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ animals were not able to form colonies in cytokine-supplemented in vitro culture as well as in spleens of host mice (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: Supported by methylcellulose assay data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: DDB1 deficient bone marrow cells were not able to form colonies in spleens of host mice.
source: Strikingly, DDB1 deficient bone marrow cells from polyI:C injected Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ animals were not able to form colonies in cytokine-supplemented in vitro culture as well as in spleens of host mice (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: Supported by CFU-S assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Deletion of Ddb1 in progenitor cells using a Cre-expressing retrovirus impaired colony formation.
source: Identical results were obtained when we deleted Ddb1 in progenitor cells using a Cre-expressing retrovirus (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by methylcellulose assay data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: All mice receiving Ddb1 deficient cells died within 3 weeks post BMT.
source: All mice receiving Ddb1 deficient cells died within 3 weeks post BMT while those receiving control cells had a normal life span (Figure 4d), indicating that Ddb1 deficient cells are not able to repopulate the hematopoietic system.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Ddb1 deficient cells are not able to repopulate the hematopoietic system.
source: All mice receiving Ddb1 deficient cells died within 3 weeks post BMT while those receiving control cells had a normal life span (Figure 4d), indicating that Ddb1 deficient cells are not able to repopulate the hematopoietic system.
evidence: Inferred from survival data and lack of engraftment shown in Figure 4d.

claim: DDB1-deficient cells (CD45.2+) lost representation in bone marrow transplant recipients.
source: DDB1-deficient cells (CD45.2+) lost representation (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: cKit+ progenitors and stem cells derived from DDB1 deficient donor cells were significantly reduced.
source: Similar to non-transplant settings, cKit+ progenitors and stem cells derived from DDB1 deficient donor cells were significantly reduced and more apoptotic as shown by AnnexinV/7AAD staining (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: cKit+ progenitors and stem cells derived from DDB1 deficient donor cells were more apoptotic.
source: Similar to non-transplant settings, cKit+ progenitors and stem cells derived from DDB1 deficient donor cells were significantly reduced and more apoptotic as shown by AnnexinV/7AAD staining (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV/7AAD staining data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The effects of Ddb1 deletion on HSPC are cell-autonomous.
source: These results further prove that the effects of Ddb1 deletion on HSPC are cell-autonomous.
evidence: Inferred from bone marrow transplant experiments showing effects persist in wild type recipients.

claim: Control cells maintained CD45.2+ chimerism through out the time course of the analysis in competitive BMT.
source: Control cells maintained CD45.2+ chimerism through out the time course of the analysis.
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood chimerism data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: DDB1-deficient cells were not able to compete with wild type counterparts in competitive BMT.
source: However, DDB1-deficinet cells were not able to compete with wild type counterparts (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood chimerism data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: DDB1-deficient myeloid cells (Mac1+Gr1+) were significantly reduced compared to wild type cells as early as 2 weeks after the Ddb1 deletion.
source: DDB1-deficient myeloid cells (Mac1+Gr1+) were significantly reduced compared to wild type cells as early as 2 weeks after the Ddb1 deletion.
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood chimerism data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: DDB1-deficient lymphoid cells (CD3+ and B220+) were reduced with slower kinetics than myeloid cells.
source: DDB1-deficient lymphoid cells (CD3+ and B220+) were also reduced with slower kinetics (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by peripheral blood chimerism data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: DDB1-deficient bone marrow displayed significant apoptosis.
source: We found that DDB1-deficient bone marrow displayed significant apoptosis (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: DDB1-deficient progenitors (both LSKs and MPs) were more apoptotic as shown by the AnnexinV staining.
source: More specifically, we found that DDB1-deficient progenitors (both LSKs and MPs) were more apoptotic as shown by the AnnexinV staining, but not lineage+ cells (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV staining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: DDB1-deficient lineage+ cells were not more apoptotic.
source: More specifically, we found that DDB1-deficient progenitors (both LSKs and MPs) were more apoptotic as shown by the AnnexinV staining, but not lineage+ cells (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV staining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: DDB1-deficient progenitor cells had elevated protein levels of phospho-Trp53, the activated form of Trp53.
source: In line with these results, DDB1-deficient progenitor cells had elevated protein levels of phospho-Trp53, the activated form of Trp53.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Cdkn1aCip1 was accumulated at the protein and mRNA levels in DDB1-deficient progenitor cells.
source: In addition, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A (Cdkn1aCip1), a transcription target of Trp53, was accumulated at the protein and mRNA levels (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Signs of DNA damage were observed in Ddb1-deficient LT-, ST-HSCs and MPPs, but not in lineage+ cells.
source: Signs of DNA damage were also observed in Ddb1-deficient LT-, ST-HSCs and MPPs, but not in lineage+ cells, as revealed by γH2Ax staining, a marker for double strand DNA breaks as well as by 53BP1 foci (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: Supported by γH2Ax staining and 53BP1 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5e,f.

claim: Trp53 deletion partially rescued the Ddb1-/- phenotype in the hematopoietic system.
source: In the hematopoietic system, Trp53 deletion partially rescued the Ddb1-/- phenotype (Figure 5g,h,i).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5g,h,i.

claim: Both the percentage and absolute number of ST-HSC (CD150+CD48+LSK), but not LT-HSC and MPP, were increased in Trp53-/-::Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ compared with Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ animals.
source: Both the percentage and absolute number of ST-HSC (CD150+CD48+LSK), but not LT-HSC and MPP, were increased in Trp53-/-::Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ compared with Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+animals (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5g,h.

claim: Trp53 activation takes place in response to Ddb1 deletion but this activation does not account for the full spectrum of the phenotype.
source: These results suggest that Trp53 activation takes place in response to Ddb1 deletion but this activation does not account for the full spectrum of the phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from partial rescue by Trp53 deletion.

claim: DDB1 was efficiently deleted at protein and mRNA levels in total thymocytes of Ddb1F/F::Cd4Cre+ mice.
source: DDB1 was efficiently deleted at protein and mRNA levels in total thymocytes (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Ddb1F/F::Cd4Cre+ mice had normal thymocyte numbers.
source: We found that these mice had normal thymocyte numbers (Figure 6c), and normal CD4/CD8 cell profiles (Figure 6d), confirming our hypothesis that Ddb1 deletion in mature/resting T cells did not affect T cell development.
evidence: Supported by cell count data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Ddb1F/F::Cd4Cre+ mice had normal CD4/CD8 cell profiles.
source: We found that these mice had normal thymocyte numbers (Figure 6c), and normal CD4/CD8 cell profiles (Figure 6d), confirming our hypothesis that Ddb1 deletion in mature/resting T cells did not affect T cell development.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: DDB1 deficient CD4+ cells failed to proliferate when activated with anti-CD3/CD28 treatment.
source: Strikingly, the DDB1 deficient CD4+ cells failed to proliferate (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation and CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: More AnnexinV positive cells were found in the culture of DDB1-deficient CD4+ cells.
source: Instead, more AnnexinV positive cells were found in the culture of DDB1-deficient CD4+ cells (Figure 6f), suggesting induction of cell death.
evidence: Supported by AnnexinV staining data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: There were significantly fewer cells incorporating EdU when Ddb1 was deleted in anti-CD3/CD28 treated cells.
source: Furthermore, we labeled anti-CD3/CD28 treated cells with EdU, an alternative of BrdU and easier for detection by immunoflourescence, and found that there were once more significantly fewer cells incorporating EdU when Ddb1 was deleted (Figure 6g,h), suggesting Ddb1 deletion interferes with cell cycle progression.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6g,h.

claim: DDB1 deficient resting cells were unable to enter S phase of the cell cycle when stimulated to proliferate.
source: Combination of BrdU and DAPI labeling clearly showed that, when stimulated to proliferate, DDB1 deficient resting cells were unable to enter S phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: Supported by BrdU and DAPI staining data.

claim: Cdkn1acip1 protein was accumulated in DDB1-deficient cells at the protein level, but not mRNA level.
source: Consistent with this result, the Cdkn1acip1 protein, a potent CDK and cell cycle inhibitor, was accumulated in DDB1-deficient cells at the protein level, but not mRNA level (Figure 6i,j).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 6i,j.

claim: Cdkn1acip1 was significantly accumulated in control cells when proteasome-dependent protein degradation was inhibited by MG132.
source: When proteasome-dependent protein degradation was inhibited by MG132, Cdkn1acip1 was significantly accumulated in control cells, however less protein accumulation following proteasome inhibition was seen in DDB1-deficient cells (Figure 6i), demonstrating that Cdkn1acip1 degradation is dependent on DDB1 function.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data with MG132 treatment shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Cdkn1acip1 degradation is dependent on DDB1 function.
source: When proteasome-dependent protein degradation was inhibited by MG132, Cdkn1acip1 was significantly accumulated in control cells, however less protein accumulation following proteasome inhibition was seen in DDB1-deficient cells (Figure 6i), demonstrating that Cdkn1acip1 degradation is dependent on DDB1 function.
evidence: Inferred from differential accumulation of Cdkn1a with proteasome inhibition shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Cdkn1acip1 was co-immunoprecipitated with Cul4 and DDB1 complex.
source: To prove direct interaction, Cdkn1acip1 was co-immunoprecipitated with Cul4 and DDB1 complex (Figure 7a), suggesting that Cdkn1acip1 is indeed a substrate of Cul4aDDB1.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Cdkn1acip1 is a substrate of Cul4aDDB1.
source: To prove direct interaction, Cdkn1acip1 was co-immunoprecipitated with Cul4 and DDB1 complex (Figure 7a), suggesting that Cdkn1acip1 is indeed a substrate of Cul4aDDB1.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: p27kip1 was not co-immuno-precipitated with the CUL4DDB1 complex.
source: In contrary, p27kip1, another cell cycle inhibitor and suggested DDB1 substrate (Bondar et al., 2006), was not co-immuno-precipitated with the CUL4DDB1 complex (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Silencing Cdkn1a did not restore stem or progenitor cell numbers in Ddb1-deficient mice.
source: To this end, Cdkn1a-/- mice were crossed to Ddb1f/f::Mx1Cre+ and polyI:C was administered. We did not observe the restoration of stem or progenitor cell numbers (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: DDB1 function is dispensable for resting T-lymphocyte homeostasis but becomes pivotal when cells enter S phase of the cell cycle.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that DDB1 function is dispensable for resting T-lymphocyte homeostasis but becomes pivotal when cells enter S phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing normal resting T cells but impaired proliferation upon activation.

claim: Silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to loss of ESC colony morphology.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to loss of ESC colony morphology (Figure 8a) and down-regulation of pluripotency factors Nanog and Oct4, and up-regulation of genes associated with mesoderm (Meox1), ectoderm (Gfap), and endoderm (Sox17) early differentiation (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: Supported by bright field images shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to down-regulation of pluripotency factors Nanog and Oct4.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to loss of ESC colony morphology (Figure 8a) and down-regulation of pluripotency factors Nanog and Oct4, and up-regulation of genes associated with mesoderm (Meox1), ectoderm (Gfap), and endoderm (Sox17) early differentiation (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 8b,c.

claim: Silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to up-regulation of genes associated with mesoderm (Meox1), ectoderm (Gfap), and endoderm (Sox17) early differentiation.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, silencing Ddb1 by shRNAs led to loss of ESC colony morphology (Figure 8a) and down-regulation of pluripotency factors Nanog and Oct4, and up-regulation of genes associated with mesoderm (Meox1), ectoderm (Gfap), and endoderm (Sox17) early differentiation (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Silencing Ddb1 in ESC did not result in aberrant cell cycle or significant change in rates of apoptosis.
source: However, we did not observe aberrant cell cycle or significant change in rates of apoptosis in these cells (Figure 8d,e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8d,e.

claim: Total Trp53 protein increased following silencing of Ddb1 in ESC.
source: Similar to ESC differentiated in the presence of retinoic acid, total Trp53 protein increased following silencing of Ddb1 (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: DDB1 is essential for ESC pluripotency and self-renewal without being accompanied by increased apoptosis or defects in cell cycle kinetics.
source: These data demonstrate that DDB1 is essential for ESC pluripotency and self-renewal without being accompanied by increased apoptosis or defects in cell cycle kinetics.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing loss of pluripotency without cell cycle or apoptosis defects.

claim: 140 proteins were identified as DDB1-interacting proteins in ESC.
source: We identified 140 proteins in ESC, 110 proteins in 293T, and 128 in HL60 cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 110 proteins were identified as DDB1-interacting proteins in 293T cells.
source: We identified 140 proteins in ESC, 110 proteins in 293T, and 128 in HL60 cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 128 proteins were identified as DDB1-interacting proteins in HL60 cells.
source: We identified 140 proteins in ESC, 110 proteins in 293T, and 128 in HL60 cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Very little overlap was found between DDB1-interacting protein subsets except CUL4A and proteins that make up the 26S proteasome.
source: Interestingly very little overlap was found between subsets except CUL4A and proteins that make up the 26S proteasome.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mass spectrometry data across cell types.

claim: In ESC, DCAF11, DCAF15, DCAF4, DCAF8 were identified as DDB1-interacting proteins.
source: In ESC we identified DCAF11, DCAF15, DCAF4, DCAF8, whereas in the hematopoietic cell line HL60 only DCAF7 was identified suggesting that differing complexes between cell types maybe responsible for the loss of DDB1 phenotype in different cell types (Figure 7a,c).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 10a,c.

claim: In the hematopoietic cell line HL60 only DCAF7 was identified as a DDB1-interacting protein.
source: In ESC we identified DCAF11, DCAF15, DCAF4, DCAF8, whereas in the hematopoietic cell line HL60 only DCAF7 was identified suggesting that differing complexes between cell types maybe responsible for the loss of DDB1 phenotype in different cell types (Figure 7a,c).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Differing complexes between cell types may be responsible for the loss of DDB1 phenotype in different cell types.
source: In ESC we identified DCAF11, DCAF15, DCAF4, DCAF8, whereas in the hematopoietic cell line HL60 only DCAF7 was identified suggesting that differing complexes between cell types maybe responsible for the loss of DDB1 phenotype in different cell types (Figure 7a,c).
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential DCAF interactions observed.

claim: Silencing of DBA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to ESC differentiation.
source: Utilizing a reporter Nanog-GFP cell line as a marker of pluripotency we identified that of the DDB1-interacting DCAF proteins found in ESC silencing of DBA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to ESC differentiation (Figure 10e).
evidence: Supported by Nanog-GFP reporter data shown in Figure 10e.

claim: Depletion of DDA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to down-regulation of transcripts associated with ESC pluripotency.
source: Furthermore, depletion of DDA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to down-regulation of transcripts associated with ESC pluripotency (Figure 10g) and lead to morphology changes consistent with differentiation (Figure 10f).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10g.

claim: Depletion of DDA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to morphology changes consistent with differentiation.
source: Furthermore, depletion of DDA1, VprBP, and DCAF11 led to down-regulation of transcripts associated with ESC pluripotency (Figure 10g) and lead to morphology changes consistent with differentiation (Figure 10f).
evidence: Supported by bright field images shown in Figure 10f.

claim: DDA1 silencing had no effect on colony formation in methylcellulose cultures of HSPC.
source: Interestingly, DDA1 silencing had no effect on colony formation in methylcellulose cultures, whereas a mild reduction in colonies was seen when VprBP was silenced.
evidence: Supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 10h.

claim: A mild reduction in colonies was seen when VprBP was silenced in HSPC.
source: Interestingly, DDA1 silencing had no effect on colony formation in methylcellulose cultures, whereas a mild reduction in colonies was seen when VprBP was silenced.
evidence: Supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 10h.

claim: Silencing of DCAF11 led to a significant (greater than 50%) reduction in colony formation in HSPC.
source: On the other hand, silencing of DCAF11 lead to a significant (greater than 50%) reduction in colony formation (Figure 10h).
evidence: Supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 10h.

claim: Different phenotypes in ESC, HSPC, and T-lymphocytes could be attributed to distinct substrate recognition by DDB1-associated DCAFs.
source: These findings suggest that different phenotypes in ESC, HSPC, and T-lymphocytes could be attributed to distinct substrate recognition by DDB1-associated DCAFs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential DCAF interactions and phenotypes observed.

claim: Ddb1 deletion affects hematopoietic progenitors by triggering DNA damage and Trp53 response, leading to the rapid induction of apoptosis.
source: Our studies suggest that Ddb1 deletion affects hematopoietic progenitors by triggering DNA damage and Trp53 response, leading to the rapid induction of apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data showing DNA damage, Trp53 activation, and apoptosis.

claim: The mechanism of CUL4-DDB1 differs depending on the cell type.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that the mechanism of CUL4-DDB1 differs depending on the cell type (Bondar et al., 2006; Cang et al., 2006; Tardat et al., 2010; Kronke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Deleting DDB1 in the early embryo is lethal, however the embryos survive till around E12.5 far past the point of the proliferation of the inner cell mass.
source: Additionally, deleting DDB1 in the early embryo is lethal, however the embryos survive till around E12.5 far past the point of the proliferation of the inner cell mass, suggesting proliferation and differentiation during early embryogenesis could be DDB1-independent (Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Proliferation and differentiation during early embryogenesis could be DDB1-independent.
source: Additionally, deleting DDB1 in the early embryo is lethal, however the embryos survive till around E12.5 far past the point of the proliferation of the inner cell mass, suggesting proliferation and differentiation during early embryogenesis could be DDB1-independent (Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of embryonic lethality.

claim: There is tissue specificity for the various CUL4-DDB1 substrates.
source: Interestingly, it appears that there is tissue specificity for the various CUL4-DDB1 substrates.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different substrates are targeted in different tissues.

claim: CDT1 and p27Kip1 appear to be targeted by the CUL4-DDB1 complex in both brain and fibroblasts.
source: CDT1 and p27Kip1 appear to be targeted by the complex in both brain and fibroblasts (Bondar et al., 2006; Cang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: c-JUN and Cdkn1acip1 are degraded by the CUL4-DDB1 complex in skin cells.
source: c-JUN and Cdkn1acip1 are degraded by the CUL4-DDB1 complex in skin cells (Cang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: PR-set7, a methyltransferase regulating replication origins, was found to be a substrate for the CUL4-DDB1 ligase.
source: More recently, PR-set7, a methyltransferase regulating replication origins, was found to be also a substrate for the CUL4-DDB1 ligase (Tardat et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ddb1 deletion resulted in accumulation of the Cdkn1acip1 protein in bone marrow progenitor populations and T lymphocytes.
source: Ddb1 deletion resulted in accumulation of the Cdkn1acip1, a CDK and cell cycle inhibitor, protein in bone marrow progenitor populations and T lymphocytes.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 5c and 6i.

claim: There was no detectable interaction between p27kip1 and the CUL4-DDB1 complex in hematopoietic cells.
source: Moreover, there was no detectable interaction between p27kip1 and the CUL4-DDB1 complex.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: It is unlikely that DDB1 exerts its function solely by regulating Cdkn1acip1 turnover in HSPC.
source: However, co-silencing Cdkn1a with Ddb1 did not rescue HSPC homeostasis, which suggests it is unlikely that DDB1 exerts its function solely by regulating Cdkn1acip1 turnover in HSPC.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of rescue by Cdkn1a deletion shown in Figure 7c.

claim: DDB1 likely controls a broader spectrum of cellular functions, through its interaction with additional novel protein substrates and the proteasome itself.
source: Indeed DNA damage and acute induction of cell death were observed upon Ddb1 deletion. Trp53 pathway silencing partially restored HSPC cell number in Ddb1-deleted animals. It is likely that DDB1 controls a broader spectrum of cellular functions, through its interaction with additional novel protein substrates and the proteasome itself (data not shown).
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete rescue by Trp53 and Cdkn1a deletion.

claim: The phenotype could be strain-dependent due to variation in MHC alleles in Trp53 and Cdkn1a rescue experiments.
source: However, it should be noted that mice with mixed background were used for Trp53 and Cdkn1a rescue experiments. The phenotype could be strain-dependent due to variation in MHC alleles.
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounding factors in the experiments.

claim: There are findings suggesting that DDB1 can exert its function independent of CUL4A/B.
source: There are findings suggesting that DDB1 can exert its function independent of CUL4A/B (Lv et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: DDB1 mainly functions as an adapter protein for the CUL4-DDB1 complex.
source: However, DDB1 mainly functions as an adapter protein for the CUL4-DDB1 complex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DDB1 function.

claim: The specificity of the CUL4-DDB1 complex comes from the DCAF family of proteins that recognize specific substrates.
source: The specificity of the complex comes from the DCAF family of proteins that recognize specific substrates.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the CUL4-DDB1 complex.

claim: Expression of DCAF proteins is cell-type specific.
source: Expression of DCAF proteins is cell-type specific and as we have shown pluripotent and adult stem cell populations vary in expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10j.

claim: Pluripotent and adult stem cell populations vary in DCAF expression.
source: Expression of DCAF proteins is cell-type specific and as we have shown pluripotent and adult stem cell populations vary in expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10j.

claim: In multiple myeloma cells treatment with lenalidomide increased ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of IKZF1 and IKZF3.
source: Interestingly, in multiple myeloma cells treatment with lenalidomide increased ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of IKZF1 and IKZF3, demonstrating that small molecules can modulate the CUL4-DDB1-DCAF complex.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Kronke et al., 2014).

claim: Small molecules can modulate the CUL4-DDB1-DCAF complex.
source: Interestingly, in multiple myeloma cells treatment with lenalidomide increased ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of IKZF1 and IKZF3, demonstrating that small molecules can modulate the CUL4-DDB1-DCAF complex.
evidence: Inferred from the lenalidomide example cited from published research.

claim: Interaction of VprBP and DDB1 was validated in 293T cells.
source: Interaction of VprBP and DDB1 was validated in 293T cells (Figure 10d).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10d.
